newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to expand range of subordinated loan lenders.
newsitem.headline: Japan to expand range of subordinated loan lenders.

text.p: Japan's Finance Ministry (MOF) may expand the range of subordinated loan lenders to help banks boost their capital bases, ministry officials say.
The ministry plans to finalise its plan this months to change its current rules limiting the scope of the lenders, they said in an interview earlier this week.
Subordinated loans are calculated as a part of bank capital under rules set under the auspices of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
At the moment, buyers of such loans are limited to life and non-life insurers, non-bank financial institutions and foreign banks.
The ministry is expected to add corporations, banks and pension funds as the lenders, the officials said.
However, to avoid cross-lending of such loans between banks, which could result in chain reaction of financial failures, the ministry will take certain measures to restrict cross-lending, they said.
The ministry may limit corporations extending subordinated loans to those which are able to raise funds from capital markets or those whose shares are listed, the officials said.
The ministry may also allow central organisations of credit associations and credit unions to provide subordinated loans to banks, they said.
Japanese banks have asked the ministry to expand the range of the lenders ahead of the introduction of the prompt corrective action (PCA) system in April, 1998.

Under the system, which gauges the financial health of banks based on the capital adequacy ratio, banks must deal with non-performing assets more strictly or risk punishment or being closed down by the authorities.
